--- title: "Exporting results" --- The frame `run_scenarios` returns does not travel as it stands, because two of its columns hold NumPy arrays rather than numbers, and an array written into a CSV cell comes back as text. The scalars and the trajectories need separate files. We write the scalar summary to one CSV, stack the trajectories into a long table, and read both back in R. The grid is the same five arms built in [A scenario grid](scenario-grid.qmd), rebuilt from the same district dictionary. ::: {#0de7b063 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pathlib import numpy as np import pandas as pd from estimint import run_scenarios, preload_models from estimint.scenarios import Scenario, EirTarget district = dict( res_use=0.30, Q0=0.85, phi=0.80, seasonal=0.0, irs=0.0, py_only=0.70, routine=0.0, eir_target=EirTarget(0.45, "prevalence"), ) grid = [ Scenario(name="Withdraw", **district), Scenario(name="Pyrethroid-only", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_only", **district), Scenario(name="PBO", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", **district), Scenario(name="Pyrrole", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pyrrole", **district), Scenario(name="PBO + IRS + LSM", itn_future=0.70, net_type_future="pyrethroid_pbo", irs_future=0.60, lsm=0.30, **district), ] res = run_scenarios(grid) ``` ::: ## An output directory `pathlib` is Python's path library. A `Path` is an object rather than a string, one that composes with the `/` operator and can make its own directory on disk. ::: {#d9b60a75 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} outputs = pathlib.Path("outputs") outputs.mkdir(exist_ok=True) outputs.resolve() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` PosixPath('/home/cosmo/Documents/Repos/MINTverse/outputs') ``` ::: ::: `exist_ok=True` makes the call idempotent, so the cell can be re-run without raising on the second pass. Paths resolve against the working directory of the session rather than the file the code sits in, and under Quarto that directory is the project root, so `outputs/` lands at the top of the project. `resolve()` prints the absolute path, which is worth reading before a long run starts writing into it. ## The scalar summary Twenty-one of the twenty-three columns are scalars, and those are the ones that belong in a spreadsheet. Drop the other two first. ::: {#ca0b0ab7 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} summary = res.drop(columns=["prevalence", "cases"]) summary.to_csv(outputs / "summary.csv", index=False) pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary.csv")[ ["name", "net_future", "dn0_future", "eir_baseline", "prev_endline", "cases_endline"] ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
name net_future dn0_future eir_baseline prev_endline cases_endline
0 Withdraw none 0.00000 31.960129 0.498149 2.127164
1 Pyrethroid-only pyrethroid_only 0.31100 31.960129 0.483688 2.433113
2 PBO pyrethroid_pbo 0.48495 31.960129 0.470118 2.412444
3 Pyrrole pyrethroid_pyrrole 0.55015 31.960129 0.464200 2.389937
4 PBO + IRS + LSM pyrethroid_pbo 0.48495 31.960129 0.038096 0.165287
``` ::: ::: `index=False` suppresses pandas' row numbers, which are an artefact of the frame rather than data and would otherwise arrive in R as a nameless leading column. Read the file straight back. It is the only way to find that a column expected to be numeric has come back as text. ## Array columns in a CSV `to_csv` takes an array column without complaint and writes the array's text representation into the cell, which is the string that printing the array would produce, brackets and line breaks included. ::: {#4b876f03 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} res.to_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv", index=False) broken = pd.read_csv(outputs / "summary-broken.csv") cell = broken.loc[0, "prevalence"] type(cell), len(cell), cell[:60] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (str, 1744, '[0.44937128 0.45082673 0.43830267 0.41571212 0.39317778 0.37') ``` ::: ::: What comes back is a single string some 1,700 characters long rather than the 157 numbers that went in. Note that no error is raised. The file is valid CSV, the column is text from then on, and anything downstream either fails on it or silently skips it. In R, `read_csv` types it as `chr` and moves on. The array is not truncated, because NumPy elides only arrays above a thousand elements and 157 is below that threshold, so every number the emulator produced is present, embedded in a single string with newlines running through it. Recovering them means parsing that string. Drop the array columns before writing instead. ::: {#b5e77f92 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} (outputs / "summary-broken.csv").unlink() ``` ::: ## Tidy format The trajectories want their own file in long form, one row per scenario per timestep, which is the shape `ggplot2` and `dplyr` expect. Recover the time grid from the emulator, then stack the arrays. ::: {#7bf7d91e .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} _, artifacts = preload_models() cfg = artifacts["prevalence"].preprocessing_config n_steps = cfg["n_steps"] abs_t = cfg["model_start_day"] + cfg["window_size"] * np.arange(n_steps) years = (abs_t - cfg["intervention_day"]) / 365 trajectories = pd.DataFrame( { "name": np.repeat(res["name"].to_numpy(), n_steps), "day": np.tile(abs_t, len(res)), "years": np.tile(years, len(res)), "prevalence": np.concatenate(res["prevalence"].to_list()), "cases": np.concatenate(res["cases"].to_list()), } ) trajectories.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` (785, 5) ``` ::: ::: `np.repeat` gives each scenario name 157 consecutive rows, `np.tile` repeats the time grid once per scenario, and `np.concatenate` on the list of arrays flattens them in the same order. Five scenarios of 157 windows is 785 rows. ::: {#7a896d73 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} trajectories.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}
name day years prevalence cases
0 Withdraw 2190 -3.000000 0.449371 2.086377
1 Withdraw 2204 -2.961644 0.450827 1.185663
2 Withdraw 2218 -2.923288 0.438303 0.658037
3 Withdraw 2232 -2.884932 0.415712 0.613480
4 Withdraw 2246 -2.846575 0.393178 0.564645
``` ::: ::: Keeping both `day` and `years` costs one column and saves an argument later. `day` is the model's own clock and is what you would join on, while `years` is centred on the campaign and is what you plot against. ::: {#29ef42eb .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} trajectories.to_csv(outputs / "trajectories.csv", index=False) sorted(p.name for p in outputs.iterdir()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` ['summary.csv', 'trajectories.csv'] ``` ::: ::: ## Reading the files in R Both files are plain CSV with a header row. Nothing about them is Python-specific. ```r library(readr) library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) summary <- read_csv("outputs/summary.csv") traj <- read_csv("outputs/trajectories.csv") summary |> select(name, net_future, dn0_future, prev_endline, cases_endline) |> arrange(prev_endline) ggplot(traj, aes(x = years, y = prevalence, colour = name)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "Years since campaign", y = "Prevalence (under 5)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal() ``` `read_csv` types the columns from the data, so `name` is a character vector and everything else a double. The `years` column puts the campaign at zero, which makes `geom_vline(xintercept = 0)` the R equivalent of the dashed campaign rule on the matplotlib figures. For a longer-lived pipeline, prefer Parquet, with `trajectories.to_parquet()` on the Python side and `arrow::read_parquet()` on the R side, which preserves the dtypes exactly and produces smaller files into the bargain. A number cannot come back as text. ## See also The analysis these two files are the output of is in [Trajectories and cases](comparing.qmd), which plots the five trajectories and integrates the clinical cases. Please see [Coming from R](../02-getting-started/coming-from-r.qmd) for pandas and dplyr side by side.
